question: Your extraction system reads vendor contracts and sets a flag_for_legal field when a clause appears non-standard. The lawyers reject most flagged clauses as routine, so the team added one sentence at the end of the system prompt: "Be conservative and only flag clauses you are highly confident about." A week of results shows almost no change in the false positive rate. What best explains why the added sentence failed to improve precision?

options.text: The sentence gives no categorical definition of a non-standard clause, so Claude still applies its own broad judgment about which clauses qualify.
options.reason: The guide states that general instructions like "be conservative" or "only report high-confidence findings" fail to improve precision compared to specific categorical criteria that define what to flag.

options.text: The sentence uses mild wording, and Claude follows precision instructions only when they are written in capital letters as strict commands.
options.reason: Stronger emphasis leaves the instruction just as general; the guide says general instructions fail because they lack specific categorical criteria, not because of their tone.

options.text: The output schema has no confidence field, so Claude has nowhere to record its certainty and cannot filter its flags by that value.
options.reason: The guide recommends specific categorical criteria rather than relying on confidence-based filtering, so adding a confidence field would not fix the missing definition.

options.text: The sentence sits at the end of a long system prompt, so lost-in-the-middle effects cause Claude to overlook it during extraction.
options.reason: The sentence is at the end, not in the middle, and the guide says that even a followed general instruction fails to improve precision because it does not define categories.
